body.hook: Every note in Western music, all twelve of them, is in the chromatic scale. Once you can play it cleanly, there's no note in your range you can't reach. That's why advanced players treat the chromatic scale as a daily workout.

study.title: The Twelve-Note Workout
study.question: How do I practise technique efficiently?
study.passage:
The chromatic scale moves in half steps. From concert B♭ up an octave: B♭ B C C♯ D E♭ E F F♯ G A♭ A B♭.
Sharps are usually used going up and flats going down, but they are enharmonic (the same pitch).
Part 1, Learn it in chunks (15 minutes): Split the octave into three chunks of four notes. Play each chunk slowly with a metronome at 60, two notes per beat. Check fingerings or slide positions on your chart, including alternate fingerings (for example, chromatic F♯ fingering on flute or the side B♭ on saxophone).
Part 2, Practice strategy (10 minutes):
1. Slow: play at a tempo where you make no mistakes.
2. Repeat correctly three times in a row.
3. Raise the metronome by 4 beats per minute.
4. If you make a mistake, go back down.
Part 3, Full scale (10 minutes): Play the full octave up and down, then extend to your range.
Part 4, Practice log: Record your starting and ending tempo and the trickiest note change.
